# Installation Guide — SMS Filter

<!-- Written By Bill Roth (bill.roth@gmail.com) — Generated by Claude — 2026-07-30 -->
<!-- Offered under the BSD 3-Clause license. Copyright (c) 2026 Bill Roth. -->

SMS Filter is distributed as an APK for private sideloading rather than through the Play Store.
This guide covers installing it on an Android phone running Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer.

## 1. Download the APK

Download `app-release.apk` to the phone, using the browser or by transferring it from a computer.
Note where it lands — usually the **Downloads** folder.

## 2. Allow installation from your browser or file manager

Android blocks installs from outside the Play Store until you permit the specific app doing the
installing.

1. Open the APK. Android will say the app is not allowed to install unknown apps.
2. Tap **Settings** in that prompt.
3. Turn on **Allow from this source**.
4. Go back and open the APK again.

You can also set this ahead of time: **Settings → Apps → Special app access → Install unknown
apps**, then pick your browser or file manager.

## 3. Get past the Play Protect warning

Play Protect scans every installed app regardless of where it came from, and shows a warning for
apps it has not seen before. This app requests SMS permissions, which raises the caution level.

When you see **"Unsafe app blocked"** or **"App scan recommended"**:

1. Tap **More details**.
2. Tap **Install anyway**.

If the option does not appear, temporarily turn off scanning at **Play Store → profile icon →
Play Protect → Settings → Scan apps with Play Protect**, install, then turn it back on. Leaving
Play Protect enabled afterwards is recommended.

The release APK is signed with a production key rather than a debug key, which is what tells Android
the package has not been tampered with since it was built.

## 4. Complete setup

Open the app and follow the three-step wizard:

1. **Welcome** — what the app does.
2. **Permissions** — grant Receive SMS, Send SMS, and Notifications. Contacts is recommended but
   optional; without it every sender is treated as unknown.
3. **Connection Test** — confirms the app can read your contacts, and tells you that auto-reply is
   ON by default.

## Things to know

These two behaviours are how Android works, not bugs in the app.

### Do not force-stop the app

If you force-stop SMS Filter from **Settings → Apps → SMS Filter → Force stop**, Android suspends
its SMS receiver entirely. It will not see another message until you open the app manually.

This also happens if a battery-optimisation tool force-stops apps on your behalf. If detections stop
happening, open the app once — that reactivates the receiver.

### Aggressive battery management can delay detection

Some manufacturers — Samsung and Xiaomi most notably — restrict background work harder than stock
Android. Detection may be delayed by seconds to minutes, or paused entirely while the phone sleeps.

To fix it, exempt the app from battery optimisation:

- **Samsung:** Settings → Apps → SMS Filter → Battery → **Unrestricted**
- **Xiaomi/Redmi/POCO:** Settings → Apps → Manage apps → SMS Filter → Battery saver → **No
  restrictions**, and enable **Autostart**
- **Stock Android/Pixel:** Settings → Apps → SMS Filter → Battery → **Unrestricted**

### Replies count against your SMS allowance

Each opt-out reply is a real text message sent from your number. The app sends at most one reply per
sender per 24 hours, which caps the volume, but the messages are billed like any other SMS.

## Uninstalling

**Settings → Apps → SMS Filter → Uninstall.** This removes the stop list, opt-out patterns,
detection log, and the stored HubSpot token. No data is held anywhere else — the app never uploads
your contacts or messages.
